evidence_quotes.quote: This is why public power never sought to impose regulations on the provision of drinking water
How could stagnant water from trenches be reconciled with that of the navigable rivers? How could it be ensured that the water that irrigated the garden would also supply the needs of the paper mill?
Water power was used not only to grind grain, but also to full cloth, saw timber, work metal and prepare paper.

The creation of a specialized magistracy in charge of the management of the water must not be understood as an interference by seigniorial power, but, on the contrary, as the response to an expectation that had been formulated for a long time.
Economic water, the water that defended, linked and nourished, the water that irrigated and made the mills turn, henceforth, passed far from the castle.

criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1: The article examines medieval and Renaissance (c. 1200-1500) hydraulic infrastructure and water uses in Milan for military defence ditches, commercial river navigation, suburban agricultural irrigation (cassine, meadows, gardens), and industrial water-powered mills (grinding grain, fulling cloth, timber, metal, paper). It explicitly states that public authorities never regulated drinking water provision or built public fountains because shallow groundwater allowed private wells, and mentions domestic wastewater channels/tanks only in a single passing sentence citing secondary literature. Per Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8, water-resource and industrial/agricultural water studies unrelated to household or community water or sanitation service access are excluded.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses legal, administrative, and governance institutions (Roman law on public rivers, communal water statutes, the giudice delle acque magistracy, water maintenance taxes on meadows/mills/barges, and Visconti/Sforza ducal licences and concessions of canal diversions). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met (no) because none of these rules or institutions govern household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access; indeed, the author explicitly states that public power never sought to impose regulations on the provision of drinking water. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criteria 1, 4, and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: Borderline/unclear: This is a narrative urban-history article drawing primarily on secondary historiography alongside illustrative citations to published medieval statutes, chronicles, and selected archival documents (ASMi, ASCM), without a formal empirical study design, sampling strategy, or systematic socio-legal analysis of service access.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: Reports historical developments in canal navigation, estate irrigation concessions (rogge), industrial mill operations, and princely political legitimation/patronage, with no household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, or affordability outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5: Does not define an eligible household/community population, service-access rule exposure, or service-access outcome within an identifiable empirical study design.

population_and_sample: Medieval and Renaissance Milan and the Lombard plain (c. 1200-1500), focusing on municipal/princely authorities, noble/monastic estate owners, merchants, and mill owners (narrative history; no sample)
exposure: Medieval communal water statutes, water magistracies (giudice delle acque), maintenance charges, and ducal canal concessions (rogge) governing navigation, estate irrigation, and water mills
outcome: Allocation, commercial/agricultural/industrial utilization, and princely political control of navigable canals, irrigation diversions, and mill water (no household or community water/sanitation service access outcome)
rationale: Exclude (E07 - Wrong service; per Exclusion Criteria 7 and 8, water-resource and industrial/agricultural water studies unrelated to household or community service access). Boucheron (2001) is a historical essay on urban and regional canals in Milan (c. 1200-1500) used for military defence ditches, commercial river navigation, suburban agricultural irrigation, and industrial water-powered mills. The paper explicitly notes that public authorities never regulated drinking-water provision or built public fountains because private groundwater wells were ubiquitous, and it reports no household or community water or sanitation service access outcomes. Under both the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 and the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded.
